title: Clinical Prior Auth, Decisions With Citations
description: A retrieval-augmented decision support system for clinical prior authorization: policy PDFs, patient charts, structured verdicts with inline citations, and the safety architecture that keeps hallucination out of medicine.

lines.text: A nurse uploads two PDFs. One is an insurance policy. One is a patient chart.
And the system says approve or deny.
It says denied, with a reason: only two weeks of documented conservative therapy. The policy requires six.
What happens if it invents that requirement?
The patient gets a denial letter citing a rule that does not exist. That is a regulatory incident.
The nurse trusted the system because it cited a specific policy page number.
But if that citation is fabricated, the trust is worse than no system at all.
This is DeployCo Take-Home, Project Teardowns. Today's project is a clinical prior-authorization assistant.
The user asks: should this be approved? The system returns approved, denied, needs more info, or insufficient evidence.
Every verdict carries inline citations back to specific pages in both documents.
My instinct is to fine tune on past decisions. Learn the pattern.
Policies change quarterly. Fine tuning bakes last quarter's rules into weights with no provenance.
Retrieval keeps truth external. Each claim traces to a page number a human can verify in seconds.
The assignment shape is retrieval-augmented generation over structured medical documents.
Scored on: does it return the right verdict, and can a human verify every claim in seconds?
So accuracy and auditability, not just fluency.

sections.title: Hybrid search over two document types

lines.text: Three concepts carry this build: hybrid retrieval, structured verdicts, and citation enforcement.
Patient charts are narrative prose. Insurance policies are numbered criteria lists.
BM25 catches exact phrases like six week conservative management. Dense embeddings catch paraphrases like non-surgical treatment first.
Hybrid search runs both and fuses results with reciprocal rank fusion.
Why not just embeddings? Policies are semantic documents.
Policy language is adversarial. Except when, must have completed, and at least six weeks are load-bearing exact terms.
Pure vector search blurs those into nearby-but-wrong sections.
Structured verdicts use Pydantic models with status, reasoning steps, citations, and next steps as separate typed fields.
Citation enforcement means every reasoning sentence must reference at least one chunk identifier from the retrieved set.
If the model cites a chunk that was not supplied, validation fails and retries or refuses.
Let me unpack each concept properly.
Hybrid retrieval means running BM25 keyword scoring and dense vector similarity independently, then merging ranked lists.
Reciprocal rank fusion computes one over sixty plus rank in each list, summed across methods.
A result ranking first in both gets a high fused score. First in one but absent from the other gets moderate score.
Why not just concatenate results and deduplicate?
Because rank information matters more than presence. A method ranking something fifth has weaker evidence than one putting it first.
For structured verdicts, Pydantic enforces types: status must be enum value, citations must be strings matching known chunk IDs.
Citation enforcement adds post-generation check: extract all chunk references from reasoning text and verify each exists in supplied evidence set.
If any reference fails validation, output is invalid. One repair retry asks model to fix only broken citation.
Walk the flow. A nurse selects a patient and hits analyze.
Step one pulls the chart from the document store. Step two reads the insurance company name from the header.
Step three filters the policy library to that payer only. Step four chunks both documents by heading boundaries and runs hybrid retrieval for the requested procedure code.
Step five sends retrieved chunks to the model with a structured-output prompt.
The model returns JSON matching the Pydantic schema. On failure, one repair retry, then refuse.
Step six renders the verdict in the UI with clickable citation links.
What about follow-up chat? Same pipeline?
Yes, but free-form questions instead of a verdict schema. Same citation requirement applies.
Chat cannot see data the analyzer did not retrieve. It shares the same evidence pool.
Now walk through a concrete example end to end.
Patient presents chronic lower back pain. Physician orders MRI lumbar spine without contrast.
Chart header shows Aetna as primary insurer. Policy filter narrows to Aetna lumbar imaging criteria.
BM25 finds exact phrase: conservative therapy for at least six weeks. Dense search finds paraphrase: non-surgical management before advanced imaging.
Both methods rank the same policy section highly. Fusion confirms it.
Patient chart retrieval finds physical therapy notes dated three weeks apart. Total documented conservative treatment approximately two weeks.
Model receives both policy criterion and chart evidence. Generates verdict denied.
Reasoning step cites policy chunk for six-week requirement and chart chunk for two-week documentation.
Recommended next steps generated: obtain four additional weeks of conservative therapy documentation, or consider peer-to-peer review.
What if the chart said approximately seven weeks instead of exactly?
That ambiguity should trigger needs-more-info rather than auto-approve. Model should flag mismatch between approximate language and hard threshold.
Clinical review tolerates seconds, not milliseconds. A three-second analysis beats a twenty-minute manual review.
But accuracy has asymmetric costs. A false approval risks harm. A false denial delays care and triggers appeals.
The system optimizes recall of relevant policy sections first, precision second.
Chunk size matters here. Whole policy sections preserve criterion numbering. Charts chunk at visit boundaries.
A lumbar imaging policy might be eight thousand tokens. Four retrieved chunks of one thousand each keeps generation manageable.
Who evaluates medical accuracy?
You cannot automate that safely with another LLM alone.
Hand-label thirty cases with a clinician. Report agreement against those labels.
Automated evals handle regression detection, not truth.
Latency breakdown for typical analysis.
Document parsing under one second per PDF using text extraction libraries. OCR adds ten to thirty seconds if needed.
Embedding generation roughly two hundred milliseconds per chunk using local sentence-transformer model.
BM25 indexing happens once at startup, updates incrementally on new documents.
Retrieval query time under fifty milliseconds for both lexical and dense paths combined.
LLM generation dominates: three to eight seconds depending on model size and output length.
Total end-to-end for typical case five to twelve seconds. Acceptable when manual review takes twenty minutes.
And cost?
Using Mistral via API roughly two cents per analysis. Self-hosted on single GPU amortizes lower at volume.
Constraint was no vector database and no LangChain. Everything runs on SQLite for metadata and in-memory arrays for embeddings.
One pass now.
Two documents enter. Both chunk by structure, not character count.
Insurance filters policies to the right payer. Hybrid retrieval finds relevant sections from both sides.
A typed model generates a verdict with per-claim citations. Validation rejects uncited claims.
Follow-up questions reuse the same evidence pool so context never drifts between views.
Full pass again with specifics.
Two documents enter: patient chart and insurance policy. Both parse into structured chunks preserving heading boundaries.
Insurance name filters policies. Hybrid retrieval scores relevance from lexical and semantic signals.
Top chunks feed the model. Structured JSON returns verdict, per-step reasoning, citations, recommendations.
Citation validator checks referenced chunks against supplied set. UI renders clickable links to source pages.
Every claim traceable in seconds.
That is the bar.

sections.title: How it breaks, and pending questions

lines.text: Failure one: scanned PDF has no text layer. Signal: zero retrieval hits on known phrases. Fix: detect and route to OCR preprocessing.
Failure two: chart mentions a different insurance company than the header. Signal: wrong payer filter. Fix: cross-reference member ID prefix against payer directory.
Failure three: procedure code maps to multiple policies with conflicting criteria. Signal: contradictory citations in output. Fix: flag for human review rather than averaging.
Pending questions before building for real: what is the liability model? Who signs off on a wrong denial?
Is PHI allowed in the LLM provider? Is there a HIPAA business associate agreement? Can you run locally or on a private endpoint?
What audit trail do regulators require? These are customer conversations before they are engineering choices.
More failure modes worth understanding deeply.
Policy PDF uses two-column layout. Naive extraction interleaves columns producing garbled sentences.
Signal: retrieval hits look relevant but reasoning quotes nonsensical text. Fix layout-aware parsing with column detection.
Patient chart contains scanned handwritten notes mixed with typed text.
Typed sections extract cleanly. Handwritten sections produce empty strings or garbage.
Signal: uneven coverage across same document. Fix flag low-quality chunks so reviewers know what was skipped.
Model hallucination despite grounding: generates plausible but incorrect medical reasoning not supported by any retrieved chunk.
Signal: citation check passes because model invents plausible-sounding chunk ID. Fix verify chunk ID exists AND quoted text appears in that chunk.
Pending questions: escalation protocol when system says insufficient evidence? Who trains nurses? What happens during API outage?
Three self-tests.
Can your system produce a verdict where every sentence traces to a page number?
If the policy changes tomorrow, how many golden cases break? Who is the human in the loop and can they override?
Fourth question: if you removed all LLM calls and kept only retrieval, could a human still find relevant policy sections faster?
If yes the LLM adds convenience on top of real value rather than being single point of failure.
Fifth: does your system distinguish between cannot find evidence and evidence says no? Those require different outputs.
Self-test: a policy says at least six weeks and the chart says approximately seven. Does the system approve?
That ambiguity boundary leads directly into conversational state: the assessment recommender next time.
What about multi-policy scenarios where patient has secondary insurance?
Genuinely unresolved coordination-of-benefits logic. Good candidate for future iteration.
